---
title: "For Students"
subtitle: "Build intuition for ML systems without GPU hardware."
---

For a student taking a first ML systems course or preparing for industry interviews, MLSys·im offers a way to experiment with real hardware specifications and see why systems behave the way they do. Hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available; outputs are derived from documented equations.

---

## Learning Objectives

Students who work through the MLSys·im tutorials learn to:

- **Identify bottlenecks**: Determine whether a workload is memory-bound or compute-bound on any hardware, and understand *why*
- **Reason quantitatively**: Use real datasheet numbers (not made-up examples) to calculate latency, throughput, and cost
- **Build systems intuition**: See how batch size, precision, parallelism strategy, and datacenter location each affect performance
- **Think across the stack**: Connect workload characteristics to hardware specs to infrastructure constraints

---

## Prerequisites

- **Python**: Comfortable with functions, loops, and f-strings
- **Math**: Basic algebra (closed-form equations using square roots, logarithms, and exponentials; no calculus required)
- **ML**: Familiarity with terms like "model parameters," "inference," and "training" (the [Glossary](glossary.qmd) defines everything else)

No GPU, no cloud account, and no special hardware are required. Installation is one command:

```bash
pip install mlsysim
```

See the [Getting Started](getting-started.qmd) guide for development installs. Local install is the supported path; Colab works by running `pip install mlsysim` in the first cell, but one-click Colab/Binder launch buttons are not available yet.

---

## Quick Start

```{python}
#| echo: true
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Load a model and hardware from the vetted registry
model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
gpu   = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# Solve: is this workload memory-bound or compute-bound?
profile = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=gpu, batch_size=1, precision="fp16", efficiency=1.0)

print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
```

---

## Predict Before Computing
Each tutorial is an executable walkthrough that pairs analytical equations with live solver code. Before inspecting the solver output in each section, estimate the expected bottleneck or scaling trend from the formula. This practice builds the mental models that effective systems reasoning depends on. The companion slide decks reinforce the same habit with 8--11 active learning moments per deck.
:::

---

## How MLSys·im Maps to the Textbook, Labs, and Slides

MLSys·im is the companion framework for the [Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai) textbook. Each solver maps to specific chapters, interactive labs, and lecture decks (see the [Cross-Volume Textbook Map](curriculum-map.qmd) for all chapters and cross-volume physics threads).

| MLSys·im Solver | What It Models | Textbook · Lab · Slides |
|:---------------|:---------------|:------------------------|
| `SingleNodeModel` | Roofline analysis, compute vs. memory bottleneck | [Vol I · Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_hw_acceleration_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-11)) |
| `TrainingMemoryModel` | Weights, gradients, Adam state, ZeRO sharding, activations | [Vol I · Ch 8: Model Training](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/08_training/08_training.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_training_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-08)) |
| `CompressionModel` | Group quantization scale overhead, pruning, accuracy delta | [Vol I · Ch 10: Model Compression](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/10_model_compression/10_model_compression.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_compression_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-10)) |

## Agentic & Physical AI Solvers (Volumes III & IV Preview)
MLSys·im also models multi-step agent horizons (`HorizonCompoundingModel`, `AcceptedTaskCostModel`, `PagedAllocationModel` in [Vol III · Ch 1](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol3/01_introduction/01_introduction.html) and [Vol III · Ch 5](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol3/05_kv_cache/05_kv_cache.html)) and cyber-physical control deadlines (`StoppingBudgetModel`, `PhaseLagBudgetModel`, `ObservationAgeModel` in [Vol IV · Ch 1](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol4/01_boundary/01_boundary.html) and [Vol IV · Ch 8](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol4/08_perception/08_perception.html)).
:::

MLSys·im is self-contained and does not require the textbook. The [Math Foundations](math.qmd) page documents the core equations, and each slide deck stands on its own with full speaker notes.

---

## Recommended Study Workflow

For self-study or a course, this workflow maximizes retention:

1. **Read** the textbook chapter (or skim the slide deck) to get the conceptual framework
2. **Predict** what will happen before running any code, and write it down
3. **Model** the setup using MLSys·im to test the prediction against real hardware specs
4. **Explore** by changing one parameter at a time (batch size, precision, hardware) and observing the effect
5. **Reflect** on where the prediction was wrong, because that gap is where learning happens

::: {.callout-note}
## Self-Study vs. Classroom
For self-study, the slide decks include **speaker notes** with timing guidance, teaching tips, and common misconceptions, written to be useful even without an instructor. In a course, the instructor may assign specific tutorials as homework; the [Instructor Guide](for-instructors.qmd) gives the recommended pairing.
:::
